title: How to evaluate a document fraud detection vendor (and why we built Inscribe the way we did)
summary: Evaluating document fraud detection software? Inscribe’s co-founder and CTO shares what to test in a pilot, from semantic analysis to network coverage.
body_markdown:
Before Inscribe, I worked at a bank. On a mortgage origination project, I saw firsthand how much time document review took. Reviewers were overwhelmed, customers were waiting on decisions, and the process was difficult to scale.


That experience was part of what led us to build Inscribe.


When people think about document fraud, they usually think about altered documents. Someone takes a legitimate document and changes something, like an address, an income figure, or an account number.


But that's just one type of document fraud. There are three others worth understanding.


- **Fabricated documents** are created from scratch, often using[templates or AI](https://www.inscribe.ai/product/ai-generated-document-fraud-detection) .
- **Stolen documents** are legitimate documents taken through unauthorized access and reused, often under a different identity.
- **Reused documents** have already been used in a previous application and are submitted again, hoping a different reviewer or institution approves them.


Each requires a different approach to detection. Stolen documents are largely detected through network intelligence. Altered documents require forensic analysis of the file itself. Fabricated documents require understanding what a legitimate document should look like, both in its structure and its content.


We've spent nine years focused exclusively on document fraud. We built Inscribe to detect all four types by looking at how a file was created, what the document says, and whether we've seen it before.


Inscribe[brings those signals together](https://www.inscribe.ai/product/overview) , explains what it found, and gives your team the evidence behind its decision. The analysis takes seconds, not minutes.


Over the years, I've heard a few questions come up repeatedly from fraud and risk teams. Here's how I'd think about each one.


## Why not keep reviewing documents by hand?


*“Our reviewers catch what comes through, and I can't justify a new tool without proof it pays off.”*


It's a fair concern.


Human reviewers are good at spotting things that look wrong. But some of the strongest indicators of fraud aren't immediately visible. They can be buried in a file's metadata, reveal themselves through small edits, or emerge when you compare information across multiple documents. It's difficult to catch those signals when you're reviewing one PDF at a time.


The tools available to fraudsters have changed, too. What once required some familiarity with tools like Photoshop can now be done with generative AI. Someone can upload a document, tell an LLM what they want to change, and get back something that looks convincing. Templates are also readily available online, making it easier than ever to create a document from scratch.


The numbers show how quickly the problem is growing. About[1 in 16 documents](https://www.inscribe.ai/reports/2026-document-fraud-report) across our network showed signs of fraud in 2025. When we got started, it was about 1 in 20. Based on the data we're recording now, we expect that to reach 1 in 15 next year.


AI-generated and template-based fraud together grew 5x in 2026. Looking at AI-generated documents alone, the[monthly number we flagged grew 4x](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/reports-ai-document-fraud-mid-year-2026) from June 2025 to May 2026, with the latest months representing the highest volumes we've recorded.


If your team has never run its documents through a specialized fraud detection tool, you may not know how much fraud you're missing. When we've analyzed a lender's past applications through Inscribe, we've found fraud they didn't know about.


Manual review is also slow and inconsistent. A single document can take minutes to review, and two reviewers can look at the same file and reach different conclusions. When someone isn't sure, the safe move is often to decline. That can mean turning away good customers and creating unnecessary friction.


Inscribe checks every document in seconds, applying the same analysis every time. Low-risk documents can move straight through. Your team gets the unusual ones, along with the evidence behind the finding, like which field changed, what it said before, and why something doesn't add up. People still make the decision. They just have better information to work with.


And this goes beyond[bank statements](https://www.inscribe.ai/solution-explorer/bank-statement-analyzer) . Inscribe analyzes[pay stubs, tax forms](https://www.inscribe.ai/document-processing/loan-document-fraud-detection) , invoices,[business filings](https://www.inscribe.ai/document-processing/kyb-document-fraud-detection) , utility bills, and other financial documents.


Connecting to bank data doesn't solve the problem either. Not everyone will share their login, and connections can fail. And if you automate document reading without checking for fraud, you risk approving fraudulent documents faster.


The quickest way to understand the difference is to try it on your own documents. Send us a sample of past applications and see what comes back.


## Why Inscribe over other document fraud vendors?


*“Every vendor says they're doing the same checks and using the most advanced AI. Their demos all look impressive, but how do I know who's actually better at detecting fraud?”*


Don't make a decision based on a demo. Run a pilot with every vendor you're seriously considering and test them against the same set of your own documents. That's the only way to understand how well each system actually performs against the fraud targeting your business.


I'd look at seven things in particular.


### 1. What does it check in the file and on the page?


The starting point for document fraud detection is forensic analysis. It looks at[metadata](https://www.inscribe.ai/document-processing/document-metadata) , layering information, previous versions, suspicious software, and inconsistencies in the file itself. It's important, but it only tells you part of the story.


Forensics is also where vendors make broad claims about handling any document, in any language, for any industry. It's easy to say you can do everything. It's harder to demonstrate which capabilities you do really well. Ask each vendor where their strengths are.


There's also visual analysis, which looks at what the document itself looks like to identify signs of manipulation. This is some of the hardest detection work to get right. Traditional techniques, like looking for differences in image compression where something was edited, produced so many false alarms that a person had to review every result. Newer vision and neural network models are changing that. We've invested heavily in this research for a long time.


### 2. Does it understand what the document says?


Semantic analysis looks at the content of a document and whether the information makes sense together. For example, someone might change their income on a bank statement but forget to update the summary box. A zip code might not match the address. Tax withholding on a pay stub might not make sense for the state listed in the address.


These inconsistencies can be easy for a person to spot when they're looking for them, but they're difficult to catch consistently at scale. Many tools in the market don't do this today. They stop at the file itself.


We've seen recall, meaning how much of the fraud we catch, improve by 10 to 20% when adding semantic analysis on top of traditional forensic signals. In a pilot, I'd specifically look at how much additional fraud a vendor catches through semantic analysis, beyond what its forensic checks already identify.


We also look beyond the document itself. We search[public web data](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/see-beyond-the-document-by-enriching-every-applicant-with-public-data) for the applicant's name, address, and business, then check what we find against the information in the document.


### 3. How quickly does your feedback change the product?


Fraud tactics change constantly. When a new tactic emerges, how long does it take your vendor to respond?


We've built Inscribe around a tight feedback loop with our customers. Customers have told us that with other vendors, it can take up to 12 months for feedback to become a product change. For us, it can take days.


Inscribe also incorporates feedback from analysts' reviews in the app, so your team's judgment helps improve detection over time.


### 4. Does the network match your business?


[Network intelligence](https://www.inscribe.ai/product/document-consortium) is one of the biggest sources of differentiation in document fraud detection.


It lets us look beyond an individual document and identify patterns across institutions. Have we seen this bank account number before under a different identity? Have we seen most of the transactions in this document associated with another identity? Does this document match what we'd expect a legitimate statement from that bank to look like, down to its metadata and fonts?


About 35% of our detections are now network-driven. Five years ago, that figure was fewer than 5%.


To evaluate a vendor's network, I'd run a pilot and measure how many fraud signals come from the network alone, where no other signals were found. That's a good way to understand what the network adds on its own, rather than just looking at the total number of flags.


Then ask how many customers like yours are in the network. Think small business lending, credit cards, consumer lending, and mortgages. How much coverage does the vendor really have? In the US, ours is very strong. It's built from activity across North American[banks](https://www.inscribe.ai/industries/banks) ,[credit unions](https://www.inscribe.ai/industries/credit-unions) ,[lenders](https://www.inscribe.ai/industries/lenders) , and fintechs, so the fraud patterns we see reflect the customers we serve.


### 5. How many good applicants will it flag?


Every wrong flag is a customer you turned away, or a file someone reviewed for nothing. Ask each vendor how many[weak signals](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/how-inscribe-uses-llms-to-reduce-false-positives-improve-document-automation) it sends you per 100 documents and what your team is supposed to do with them. We focus on the signals that actually predict fraud.


### 6. Can you adjust it to how your team works?


Every institution has a different risk appetite, customer base, and review process. A fraud detection system needs to account for those differences.


About 80% of the configuration is consistent across customers. The remaining 20% is where you can tailor the system to your business and standard operating procedures. You can adjust how strict the system is and[build your own checks](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/how-to-turn-your-teams-fraud-expertise-into-automated-checks) across documents and transactions.


### 7. Can your team act on what it finds?


Inscribe explains the reasons behind every finding[in plain language](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/explainable-ai-fraud-detection-vendor-guide) , so reviewers, sales teams, and partners can understand what happened without digging through raw data.


The goal isn't just to flag more documents. It's to help your team make better decisions without creating more work.


### The bottom line


Compare vendors on how much fraud they catch, how many legitimate documents they flag, and how useful their findings are to your team. Don't just take a vendor's word for it. Make them prove it with your data.


## Why not build it yourself with an LLM?


*“We have a great engineering team and access to the most advanced LLMs. Why couldn't we just build this ourselves?”*


It's a reasonable question, and we use LLMs ourselves. But there's a big difference between asking a[general-purpose model](https://www.inscribe.ai/blog/when-does-it-make-sense-to-use-an-llm) whether a document looks suspicious and building a system that can reliably detect document fraud at scale.


An LLM can tell you whether a document looks plausible. But plausibility isn't the same as authenticity. A convincing fraudulent document is specifically designed to look legitimate. A model needs more than the document's visible contents to determine whether it's real.


It needs to understand how the file was created and edited, whether the information makes sense, and whether the document matches what a legitimate statement from that institution should look like. It also needs to know whether the same document or underlying information has appeared before.


Then there's the data. An institution building its own system primarily sees the fraud targeting its own business. Inscribe learns from fraud patterns across a network of North American financial institutions, lenders, and fintechs.


And the detection model is only one part of the equation. You also need scoring, explanations, review workflows, monitoring, and ongoing tuning as fraud tactics evolve. That requires a team of engineers, data scientists, and fraud analysts working together.


That's what we've spent nine years building at Inscribe. We use LLMs within our detection system, alongside specialized detectors, network intelligence, and fraud research. Our risk operations team continually updates those capabilities as new tactics emerge.


A year ago, some AI-generated documents were relatively easy to spot. That's no longer the case. As the tools for creating convincing fraudulent documents improve, detection needs to keep pace. Building and maintaining that capability is a much bigger undertaking than writing a prompt.


## First to market, still focused on one problem


I started with reviewers who were overwhelmed and customers waiting on decisions. That's still the problem we care about. Fraud keeps changing, and the people fighting it shouldn't have to do it by hand, one document at a time.


We were the[first vendor](https://www.inscribe.ai/about) to bring document fraud detection to market, and we've spent nine years focused only on it. Being first gave us a head start on learning from real document fraud. We look at the whole document, not just the file. We learn from fraud across institutions. And we move quickly when something new shows up, because in this space, how fast detection keeps up matters as much as what it catches today.
